title: What science taught
hook: attention, habit and compassion can grow, modestly

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was a year of thinkers: Lao Tzu, Montaigne, Emerson and Thoreau, one line each. Your line was four lines.

Somewhere in the middle of this year, the path left the old books for the lab. Monks in brain scanners. A gorilla walking unseen through a room of people passing basketballs. Habit curves, urge surfing, people in a hurry passing someone in need. Then a hard turn: the replication crisis, and a long look at which famous findings held up and which didn't. Today asks a simpler question, the kind a friend asks over dinner: so what did science actually teach you? Not the headlines. The modest, honest summary you'd still stand behind.
screen: `FROM THE OLD BOOKS TO THE LAB.` → `WHAT HELD UP, WHAT DIDN'T.` → `THE MODEST SUMMARY.`

segments.voice: Three things, and one word that goes with all of them. First, attention. It's limited, and it wanders. The studies this path looked at suggest it can be trained, a little, with practice: returning, again and again, is the exercise. Second, habit. Habits live in cues and places, they form through repetition, and a missed day doesn't erase the curve. The psychologist William James, in his Principles of Psychology, put the idea in one sentence: "The great thing, then, in all education, is to make our nervous system our ally instead of our enemy." Repetition is how an ally is made. Third, compassion. The research suggests compassion can be practiced, not only felt, and that practice can shift it somewhat. And the one word for all three: modestly. This year also taught where the claims went too far. Some celebrated results didn't hold up when others tried them again. Some effects were smaller than the headlines. Mindfulness isn't a cure-all, and it can be hard for some people. That honesty is part of the lesson, not a footnote. So the summary isn't "meditation rewires everything." It's quieter, and sturdier. Attention, habit and compassion behave more like muscles than fixed traits. They respond to steady, ordinary practice, by small amounts, over time. Which means a useful kind of evidence about your own practice is in your own life: what, this year, actually grew?
screen: `ATTENTION CAN BE TRAINED, A LITTLE.` · `HABIT: MAKE THE NERVES AN ALLY.` · `COMPASSION CAN BE PRACTICED.` · `MODESTLY.` · then, large: `WHAT, THIS YEAR, GREW?`

segments.voice: Think back to where you were at the start of this year, and ask three quiet questions. Is your attention any steadier, even a little? Is there one habit that holds now that didn't before, or someone you're kinder to? Don't measure or argue with yourself; just notice one small thing that grew, and let yourself see it.
What science taught. Attention, habit and compassion can grow with practice, modestly, and some big claims didn't hold up. Today's word.
Your line: it grew. Small changes, by small amounts over time, still count. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Careful researchers who study contemplative practice describe its effects on attention, habit and compassion as real but modest, and call for replication; practitioners who want to track their own change sometimes keep a simple journal.
